P3Q1.q: According to Aquinas, what is the formal object of faith — that by which everything else believed is held?
options: Sacred Scripture read literally
The First Truth (God's own truth)
The teaching authority of bishops
Conclusions proven by natural reason
P3Q1.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the material object of faith (the many things believed) from its formal object, the First Truth, through which all particular truths of faith are believed.

P3Q1.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that nothing false can ever be an object of faith?
options: Because Church councils have declared Scripture inerrant
Because the formal aspect of faith's object is the First Truth, under which nothing false can stand
Because believers only assent to things demonstrated by reason
Because faith requires visible proof before assent
P3Q1.explanation: Just as non-being cannot stand under being, nothing false can stand under the First Truth, which is the formal aspect under which everything believed is held.

P3Q1.q: Why, according to Aquinas, does the authority to publish a new edition of the Creed belong solely to the Sovereign Pontiff?
options: Because he alone can read the original Greek councils
Because he has final authority to decide matters of faith, so the whole Church may hold one faith without schism
Because early councils delegated this specific task to Rome by vote
Because only he is free from the possibility of heresy
P3Q1.explanation: Aquinas argues that settling questions of faith for the whole Church requires one who presides over the whole Church, so that all may hold firmly to a single decision and avoid schism.

P3Q2.q: What three reasons does Aquinas give for why it is necessary to believe even truths about God that could, in principle, be proved by reason?
options: Tradition, obedience, and humility
Faster and more general access to divine knowledge, plus greater certitude than unaided reason provides
Simplicity, brevity, and memorability
Scriptural inerrancy, papal authority, and conciliar decree
P3Q2.explanation: Aquinas gives three motives: reaching knowledge of God more quickly (since proving God's existence presupposes many sciences), making it available to all regardless of ability, and securing certainty, since philosophers reasoning alone fell into many errors.

P3Q2.q: Why does Aquinas hold that the act of believing can be meritorious?
options: Because it requires great intellectual effort
Because it is an act of the intellect assenting to divine truth at the command of the will moved by grace, and so is subject to free will directed toward God
Because belief is always accompanied by visible miracles
Because it fulfills a legal precept of the Church
P3Q2.explanation: Since meritorious acts proceed from free will moved by grace and referred to God, and the act of faith is precisely such an act of intellect commanded by a grace-moved will, believing can be meritorious.

P3Q2.q: According to Aquinas, when do human reasons offered in support of what one believes diminish the merit of faith, and when do they increase it?
options: They always diminish merit, since faith should never involve reasoning
They diminish merit when the will requires them before it is willing to believe, but increase merit when sought after the will is already disposed to believe
They always increase merit, since reasoning is superior to blind assent
They are irrelevant to merit in every case
P3Q2.explanation: Reasons that precede and are necessary to produce the will's assent lessen the merit, since one ought to believe for God's authority rather than human argument; but reasons sought once the will already loves and believes the truth are a sign of greater merit.

P3Q3.q: Why does Aquinas classify outward confession of faith as an act of the virtue of faith itself, rather than of some other virtue?
options: Because confession requires courage, making it an act of fortitude instead
Because outward actions belong to the virtue to whose end they are specifically directed, and confession's proper end is to manifest inward faith
Because confession is commanded directly by charity
Because it is primarily a liturgical act governed by religion
P3Q3.explanation: Aquinas's principle is that an outward act belongs to the virtue whose end it specifically serves (as fasting serves abstinence); confession serves specifically to express and profess the belief held within, so it belongs to faith.

P3Q3.q: According to Aquinas, is confessing one's faith outwardly obligatory at every single moment for salvation?
options: Yes, silence about one's faith is always a mortal sin
No — like other affirmative precepts, it binds always (is permanently in force) but not for always (i.e., not at every instant), depending on time, place, and circumstance
No, confession of faith is never strictly obligatory
Yes, but only for clergy, not laypeople
P3Q3.explanation: Aquinas applies his general teaching on affirmative precepts: they oblige semper (always, in principle) but not pro semper (at every moment), so confession is required at due times and circumstances, not continuously.

P3Q3.q: What kind of precept, in Aquinas's analysis, governs the obligation to confess one's faith?
options: A negative precept forbidding denial only under torture
An affirmative precept, since confession is something affirmative (a positive declaration)
A merely counseled, non-binding practice
A precept belonging strictly to canon law, not divine law
P3Q3.explanation: Aquinas notes that since confession of faith is something affirmative, its necessity for salvation falls under an affirmative precept of divine law, which governs how and when it binds.

P3Q4.q: In Aquinas's analysis of Hebrews 11:1, why must faith reside as a habit in both the intellect and the will?
options: Because faith is purely an emotional disposition
Because the act of believing proceeds from two active principles — intellect and will — and a perfect act arising from two principles requires each to be perfected by its own habit
Because Scripture explicitly names two virtues
Because the intellect alone cannot hold any belief without external proof
P3Q4.explanation: Since to believe is an act of intellect that assents because the will moves it, and a perfect act from two principles needs a perfecting habit in each, faith as a virtue must reside in the intellect while being moved by the will.

P3Q4.q: According to Aquinas, in what sense is charity called the "form" of faith?
options: Charity literally changes the intellectual content of what is believed
Charity, as the will's proper act directed to the Divine good (faith's end), perfects and shapes the act of faith the way a form gives a thing its species
Charity is identical to faith, just under another name
Charity is required only for lifeless, not living, faith
P3Q4.explanation: Because a voluntary act's form is the end to which it is directed, and faith's act is ordered to the Divine Good which is charity's proper object, charity is said to inform or perfect the act of faith, making it 'living' faith.

P3Q4.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that living faith is truly a virtue?
options: Because it is infused directly without any act of will
Because its act requires the intellect to tend infallibly to the true and the will (through charity) to be directed to a good end — both conditions of a virtuous human act
Because it produces visible miracles in the believer
Because it is identical with the theological virtue of hope
P3Q4.explanation: A human virtue is a habit that is always the principle of a good act; living faith meets this because the intellect assents to the true and, formed by charity, the will is rightly ordered to the last end.

P3Q5.q: Why does Aquinas hold that Adam and the angels, before sin or confirmation in grace, still possessed faith rather than the vision of God?
options: Because they had no knowledge of God whatsoever
Because faith is excluded only by the vision that gives the happiness of seeing God's essence, which neither Adam nor the unconfirmed angels yet possessed
Because Scripture explicitly calls Adam a believer
Because angels cannot know spiritual truths without revelation
P3Q5.explanation: Since faith is 'the evidence of things that appear not,' only the beatific vision of the First Truth excludes it; lacking that vision, both unconfirmed angels and pre-lapsarian man still had faith rather than sight.

P3Q5.q: How does Aquinas explain that demons can be said to "believe" while still lacking true faith as a virtue?
options: Demons believe because they love the good that is proposed
Their intellects are compelled to assent by evidence of signs (like miracles) that convince them God is speaking truly, even though this assent does not proceed from a will directed to the good
Demons have no intellect capable of assent
Demons possess living faith formed by charity
P3Q5.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes assent moved by a will directed to good (praiseworthy belief) from assent forced upon the intellect by convincing but unloved evidence; demons' 'belief' is of the second kind, lacking the virtue of faith.

P3Q5.q: According to Aquinas, what happens to a person's faith in the other articles if he obstinately disbelieves just one article of the faith?
options: He retains full living faith in all other articles
Neither living nor lifeless faith remains in him regarding the other articles, since he no longer holds them on the formal ground of divine authority
He becomes an atheist automatically
His faith becomes stronger in the remaining articles
P3Q5.explanation: Because faith's formal object is the First Truth as revealed, rejecting one article on one's own judgment undermines the very ground (God's authority) on which all the others are held, so genuine faith in any of them is lost.

P3Q6.q: Why does Aquinas insist that faith must be infused into man by God rather than acquired solely by human effort?
options: Because faith requires no proposal of truths at all
Because the truths of faith surpass human reason and so cannot come to man's knowledge unless God reveals them, whether immediately or through preachers He sends
Because human reason is entirely incapable of any true knowledge
Because infused faith replaces the need for preaching
P3Q6.explanation: Aquinas notes two requirements for faith — the proposal of truths and interior assent — and since matters of faith exceed reason, their being made known at all depends on God's revelation, directly or through those He sends.

P3Q6.q: How does Aquinas explain that even "lifeless" (unformed) faith is still a gift of God, despite lacking charity?
options: Because lifelessness (lack of charity) is not essential to the very species of the habit of faith, so God can still be the cause of faith even where charity's supervening privation is absent
Because lifeless faith is a natural, not supernatural, habit
Because charity is unnecessary for any act of faith
Because lifeless faith is caused entirely by the sinner's own will
P3Q6.explanation: Aquinas argues by analogy with darkness in a diaphanous body: privation not essential to a thing's species doesn't need the same cause as the thing itself, so God can be cause of the habit of faith even in its lifeless (uninformed) state.

P3Q7.q: According to Aquinas, how does faith give rise to servile fear?
options: Faith removes all fear from the believer
Faith produces an apprehension of penal evils that God's judgment may inflict, and this apprehension of evil is the principle from which the fear of being punished arises
Fear arises independently of any belief in divine judgment
Servile fear is a fruit of charity, not of faith
P3Q7.explanation: Since every appetitive movement like fear begins from an apprehension of good or evil, and faith gives us apprehension of the punishments of divine judgment, faith becomes the source of servile (fear-of-punishment) fear.

P3Q7.q: Why does Aquinas say faith is the "first beginning" of the heart's purification, even though it is not sufficient by itself?
options: Because faith alone, without charity, fully purifies the heart
Because purification begins with turning toward God, which starts with believing that He exists (per Hebrews 11:6), though perfect purification requires faith to be quickened by charity
Because purification is entirely accomplished by good works, not faith
Because faith removes all attachment to bodily things automatically
P3Q7.explanation: The heart becomes impure by loving transient things and is purified by the contrary movement toward God; since 'he who comes to God must believe,' faith initiates this movement, and charity perfects it.

P3Q8.q: How does Aquinas explain the meaning of "understanding" as a gift of the Holy Ghost?
options: It refers only to logical deduction from premises
It signifies an intimate, penetrating knowledge ("intus legere," to read inwardly) that grasps the very essence of a thing, unlike sense knowledge which stays at external qualities
It is identical to the gift of wisdom with no real distinction
It applies only to knowledge of physical creatures, not God
P3Q8.explanation: Aquinas derives 'intelligere' from 'intus legere' (to read within), contrasting the intellect's penetration to a thing's essence with sense knowledge's limitation to external, sensible qualities.

P3Q8.q: According to Aquinas, is the gift of understanding compatible with faith, given that faith concerns the unseen?
options: No, understanding and faith are mutually exclusive habits
Yes — properly distinguished, the gift of understanding gives a certain penetrating grasp of truths still held by faith without yet reducing them to the clear vision that would eliminate faith
Understanding replaces faith entirely once received
Faith and understanding differ only in the persons who possess them, not in kind of knowledge
P3Q8.explanation: Aquinas resolves the apparent conflict by distinguishing senses of 'faith' and 'understanding,' concluding the gift gives deeper penetration into believed truths without turning faith into full sight.

P3Q8.q: Why, according to Aquinas, must a person be in a state of grace to truly possess the gift of understanding directed to the right end?
options: Grace is irrelevant to the gift of understanding

Grace rightly disposes the will to good, but the will needs prior knowledge of truth to be so directed, and the Holy Ghost's gift of understanding supplies that supernatural knowledge of the true end that the rightly-disposed will requires
Understanding operates independently of both will and grace
Only those without sanctifying grace can receive the gift of understanding
P3Q8.explanation: Because the will's rectitude toward good presupposes some grasp of truth (the will's object is a good understood), the Holy Ghost enlightens the mind through the gift of understanding so the right will has a true end to which to tend.

P3Q9.q: Why does Aquinas say the gift of knowledge perfects man in two distinct ways when he assents to a truth by natural reason?
options: Only by making him certain, never by helping him grasp it
By enabling him to grasp the truth and also to form a sure, right judgment about it, since grace does not fail to perfect what nature already begins
By eliminating the need for any judgment at all
By replacing natural reason entirely with revealed doctrine
P3Q9.explanation: Since grace is more perfect than nature and does not fail where nature can be perfected, the gift of knowledge, like natural assent, perfects man both in grasping a truth and in judging rightly about it.

P3Q9.q: According to Aquinas, why is the order of judgments in the gift of knowledge modeled on the order of causes?
options: Because judgments about causes are arbitrary and unordered

Because a sure judgment about a thing is formed chiefly from its cause, so judging the second cause should be done through the first cause, making judgment through the first cause the most perfect judgment
Because Aquinas denies that causes have any bearing on certainty
Because the gift of knowledge concerns only effects, never causes
P3Q9.explanation: Aquinas reasons that certainty of judgment tracks causal order — the more fundamental the cause invoked, the surer and more perfect the judgment, culminating in judgment through the first cause.

P3Q9.q: How does the third beatitude, "Blessed are they that mourn," correspond to the gift of knowledge in Aquinas's account?
options: Mourning has no connection to knowledge of creatures
Right judgment about creatures (proper to the gift of knowledge) reveals that placing one's last end in creatures is a loss, and recognizing this loss is a fitting cause of mourning
The beatitude concerns only mourning for the dead
Aquinas denies any beatitude corresponds to the gift of knowledge
P3Q9.explanation: Because a wrong judgment placing final good in creatures leads to a real loss, the right judgment about creatures that the gift of knowledge provides makes a person aware of that loss, prompting the mourning of the third beatitude.

P3Q10.q: According to Aquinas, in what sense is unbelief properly a sin, as opposed to a mere lack of faith?
options: Any absence of faith, even through no fault of one's own, is equally sinful
Unbelief is sinful specifically when taken as opposition to the faith — refusing to hear or despising it — not merely as the pure negation of never having heard it
Unbelief is never sinful under any description
Sin only applies to unbelief among the baptized
P3Q10.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes unbelief as pure negation (simply not having faith, e.g. never having heard it) from unbelief as opposition or contempt toward the faith; only the latter completes the notion of sin.

P3Q10.q: Why does Aquinas locate the sin of unbelief in the intellect, even though the will is its first mover?
options: Because the will has no role in unbelief at all

Because while the will is the universal principle commanding every sin, the proximate and proper principle eliciting the specific act — dissent from revealed truth — is the intellect, moved by the will
Because sin can never be located in a single power
Because unbelief is purely a bodily, not a spiritual, disorder
P3Q10.explanation: Aquinas's general principle is that sin is located in the power that is its proper elicitive principle; since dissent (unbelief's proper act) is an act of intellect moved by will, unbelief's subject is the intellect, as assent is for faith.

P3Q10.q: Why does Aquinas judge the unbelief of heretics to be a graver sin than that of Jews or pagans who never accepted the Gospel?
options: Because heretics are punished more severely by civil law

Because resisting the faith after having accepted it is a graver betrayal — like breaking a promise once made — whereas those who never accepted it (or accepted only its Old Law figure) have not broken such a commitment
Because heretics lack any natural knowledge of God
Aquinas holds all forms of unbelief are equally grave
P3Q10.explanation: Aquinas reasons that resisting faith already accepted is worse than never accepting it, similar to breaking a promise; heretics corrupt a faith they professed, making their unbelief graver than that of Jews or pagans who never professed the Gospel faith.

P3Q11.q: According to Aquinas, why does heresy specifically involve "choosing" (from which its name derives)?
options: Because heretics choose to leave the Church building

Because choice concerns things directed to a presupposed end, and heretics treat secondary truths as if they, not the First Truth, were the end, selecting which teachings to accept according to their own will
Because heresy always involves choosing a new religion entirely
Choice has no real connection to the meaning of heresy for Aquinas
P3Q11.explanation: Aquinas links heresy to choice: since the will assents to the First Truth as its proper good/last end, heresy involves the will selecting some secondary matter of faith on private judgment rather than accepting it as ordered to that end.

P3Q11.q: Why does Aquinas say a false opinion about geometry is not heresy, while a false opinion about the Trinity is?
options: Because geometry is more difficult than theology
Because heresy specifically denotes corruption of the Christian faith, so only false opinions about matters actually belonging to the faith count, not unrelated fields like geometry
Because heresy applies to any false belief whatsoever
Because Aquinas denies that any subject outside faith can be held falsely
P3Q11.explanation: Aquinas restricts heresy to false opinions specifically about things belonging to the faith; error in unrelated matters, like geometry, does not corrupt the faith and so is not heresy.

P3Q11.q: What is Aquinas's stated rationale for why heretics, once convicted, may be handed over to death by secular authority?
options: Because heresy is a purely political crime
Because corrupting the faith that gives life to the soul is a graver matter than counterfeiting money, and forgers are already justly put to death, so heretics deserve no less
Because heretics are automatically guilty of violence
Because it is the only way to prevent heresy from spreading demographically
P3Q11.explanation: Aquinas argues by comparison: if civil authorities justly execute counterfeiters for corrupting temporal currency, there is much greater reason to punish heretics who corrupt the faith that gives life to the soul.

P3Q12.q: How does Aquinas distinguish apostasy from religious life or Holy Orders from apostasy from the faith itself?
options: They are identical, since both are called apostasy

Man is united to God in several ways (faith, obedience to commandments, and works of supererogation like religious life); withdrawing from a later, less fundamental union (like religious profession) does not necessarily remove the more fundamental union of faith
Apostasy from Orders is impossible once ordained
Apostasy always includes loss of faith by definition
P3Q12.explanation: Aquinas notes that removing what follows (like a vow of religious life) does not remove what precedes it (faith); so one can apostatize from religious life or Orders while remaining united to God by faith.

P3Q12.q: According to Aquinas, does a prince automatically lose his right to rule the moment he becomes an apostate from the faith?
options: Yes, unbelief automatically annuls all human legal rights instantly

No — dominion is grounded in human law (the law of nations), which the distinction of believer/unbeliever (a matter of divine right) does not automatically annul, though he may be justly sentenced to lose it as a punishment
Yes, because only believers can legitimately hold any authority under natural law
No, apostate princes retain authority permanently with no possibility of forfeiture
P3Q12.explanation: Aquinas reasons that dominion arises from human law, unaffected automatically by the divine-right distinction between believers and unbelievers, but civil or ecclesiastical authority may still justly sentence an apostate prince to lose his rule as a penalty.

P3Q13.q: How does Aquinas define the essence of blasphemy?
options: Any harsh criticism of Church leaders
The disparagement of some surpassing goodness, especially God's, by denying what befits Him or affirming what does not befit Him
Only the literal utterance of a forbidden divine name
A purely liturgical offense against ritual language
P3Q13.explanation: Since God is essential goodness itself, whatever is unbefitting Him detracts from that goodness; blasphemy is precisely this disparagement, whether by false denial or false affirmation about God.

P3Q13.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that blasphemy is always a mortal sin by reason of its genus?
options: Because it is punished by civil law
Because it is directly opposed to charity, since it disparages the Divine goodness which is charity's very object, and whatever is contrary to charity is mortal in its genus
Because it always involves scandal to others
Because Scripture lists it among ritual, not moral, offenses
P3Q13.explanation: Mortal sin severs one from charity, the principle of spiritual life; because blasphemy by its nature disparages the Divine goodness that is charity's object, it is opposed to charity and thus mortal in its genus.

P3Q13.q: According to Aquinas, in what sense do the damned in hell "blaspheme" God?
options: They do not blaspheme, since they cannot sin further after death

Their persistent detestation of God's justice — hating their punishments while still loving the sins for which they are punished — constitutes an interior blasphemy of the heart, likely voiced aloud after the resurrection
They blaspheme only verbally, never internally
They blaspheme because they no longer believe God exists
P3Q13.explanation: Aquinas holds the damned retain a wicked will turned from God's justice, hating their punishment while still loving their sins; this ongoing detestation is itself blasphemy of heart, which he thinks will become vocal after the resurrection.

P3Q14.q: How does Aquinas explain the Pharisees' progression from blaspheming "the Son of Man" to blaspheming against the Holy Ghost, per Matthew 12?
options: There is no real distinction between the two blasphemies

They first mocked Christ's ordinary human actions (eating, drinking), but then attributed His divine works (done by the Holy Ghost's power) to the devil, which is blasphemy against the Holy Ghost specifically
Blasphemy against the Holy Ghost refers only to sins committed by clergy
The distinction concerns only which day of the week the blasphemy occurred
P3Q14.explanation: Aquinas explains that Christ's human acts belonged to His human nature, while His divine works (exorcisms, raising the dead) were done by the Godhead and the Holy Ghost; the Pharisees blasphemed against the Holy Ghost specifically by ascribing those divine works to the devil.

P3Q14.q: In Aquinas's third and fullest sense of "sin against the Holy Ghost," what unifies the six kinds he distinguishes (like despair and presumption)?
options: They are all sins of ignorance rather than malice
Each removes some safeguard against sin — grounded in God's judgment, His gifts, or the nature of sin itself — such as hope removed by despair or fear removed by presumption
They are all purely verbal sins
They apply only to sins committed in anger
P3Q14.explanation: Aquinas organizes the six species around the contemptuous rejection of things that would normally hinder sin through choice — for example, presumption removes the fear grounded in God's justice, and despair removes the hope grounded in His mercy.

P3Q14.q: Why can final impenitence be called an "unpardonable" sin against the Holy Ghost in Aquinas's account, without denying that God's mercy is infinite?
options: Because God arbitrarily refuses to forgive certain sins
Because it is unpardonable in the sense that a mortal sin persisted in until death is never in fact remitted, since it was not repented of in this life, not because God's power to forgive is limited
Because it refers to a sin committed only by non-Christians
Because Aquinas denies final impenitence exists as a category
P3Q14.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that calling final impenitence unpardonable describes the fact that no repentance intervenes before death to receive forgiveness, not a restriction on the scope of divine mercy itself.

P3Q15.q: How does Aquinas define "blindness of mind" as a sin?
options: An involuntary neurological condition with no moral character

A privation of one of the principles of intellectual sight — through fault, one becomes unable to perceive truths he otherwise could, distinct from cases like imbecility where natural reason is merely hindered without fault
A synonym for original sin itself
A condition affecting only unbelievers, never the faithful
P3Q15.explanation: Aquinas treats blindness of mind by analogy to bodily blindness, as a privation of a principle of intellectual sight; where this privation results from culpable causes (like vice) rather than natural incapacity, it counts as sin.

P3Q15.q: According to Aquinas, why does he distinguish "dulness of sense" from "blindness of mind" using the metaphor of piercing?
options: He does not actually distinguish them

Dulness, by metaphor from the bodily senses' ability to "pierce" to fine or distant details, denotes an inability of the mind to penetrate to the subtler or higher truths, distinct from blindness which is a fuller privation of intellectual sight
Dulness refers only to physical hearing loss
The two terms are used interchangeably throughout the article
P3Q15.explanation: Aquinas uses the sense-based metaphor of sharpness (ability to pierce to distant or minute objects) versus dullness (limited to what is near or obvious) to describe a lesser defect of penetrating insight, distinguished from the fuller privation called blindness.

P3Q15.q: Why does Aquinas connect blindness of mind and dulness of sense to sins of the flesh, such as gluttony and lust?
options: Fleshly sins have no bearing on intellectual operation

Perfect intellectual operation requires abstraction from sensible phantasms, but pleasure fixes a person's attention on what he enjoys, so indulgence in bodily pleasure hinders the mind's ability to attend to and penetrate intelligible truths
Only sins of anger affect the intellect, according to Aquinas
Bodily sins strengthen intellectual clarity by comparison
P3Q15.explanation: Because intellectual operation depends on detachment from sensory phantasms, and pleasure rivets attention on its object, indulgence in carnal pleasures (paradigmatically lust) impedes the mind's capacity for clear intellectual consideration, producing blindness or dulness.

P3Q16.q: Why, according to Aquinas, must faith be presupposed before the precepts of the Old Law can be given?
options: Because faith is itself one of the Ten Commandments

Because a lawgiver only binds his own subjects, and man's primary subjection to God is through faith (per Hebrews 11:6), so faith is presupposed before legal precepts — reflected in the declaration "I am the Lord thy God" preceding the commandments
Because the Israelites required faith only after receiving the Law, not before
Because Aquinas denies any precepts of faith existed under the Old Law
P3Q16.explanation: Since precepts of a law presuppose subjects already under the lawgiver, and man becomes subject to God chiefly through faith, faith is logically and textually prior to the legal precepts, as shown by the declaration of God's identity preceding the commandments in Exodus.

P3Q16.q: According to Aquinas, what three aspects of knowledge and understanding does the Old Law's precepts address?
options: Only their preservation, ignoring reception and use
Their reception (through teaching and learning), their use, and their preservation
Only memorization techniques
Their reception alone, with use and preservation left unaddressed
P3Q16.explanation: Aquinas identifies three aspects addressed by precepts concerning knowledge and understanding — how they are received via teaching and learning, how they are used, and how they are to be preserved — citing Deuteronomy's commands to keep God's words in the heart and teach them to one's children.

P3Q17.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that hope is genuinely a virtue?
options: Because hope is merely a natural passion common to all animals
Because a human act is good when it attains its due measure — reason or God — and the act of hope attains God Himself by leaning on His help to obtain a future, arduous, but possible good
Because hope requires no cooperation from grace
Because it is listed as a virtue by the Philosopher, with no further rational grounds
P3Q17.explanation: Aquinas argues that since hope, as he treats it here, reaches for a good attainable through divine assistance, it attains God as its 'rule,' making the act — and therefore the habit that produces it — genuinely virtuous.

P3Q17.q: According to Aquinas, why is eternal happiness specifically the proper and principal object of theological hope?
options: Because eternal happiness is simply one desirable good among many equally valid objects of hope

Because an effect must be proportionate to its cause, and since God's help is infinite in power, the good properly hoped for from Him is the infinite good — eternal life, the enjoyment of God Himself — not anything less
Because Aquinas holds hope concerns only temporal, this-worldly rewards
Because eternal happiness is only a secondary, not principal, object of hope
P3Q17.explanation: Since hope leans on God's infinite power to attain the hoped-for good, and effect must match cause, the fitting object of hope from God is nothing less than Himself — eternal life and the enjoyment of God — making this its proper and principal object.

P3Q17.q: How can Aquinas say one may hope for another person's eternal happiness, given that hope's direct object is one's own good?
options: He denies this is possible under any circumstances

Hope directly regards one's own good, but presupposing the union of love (charity) with another, one can extend hope to another as to a kind of second self, just as the same charity loves God, self, and neighbor
Hoping for another's happiness is classified as an act of faith, not hope
One can only hope for another's happiness if that person is a blood relative
P3Q17.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes love, which unites us to another as another self, from hope, which is a movement toward one's own arduous good; but once love's union is presupposed, hope can extend to another's good as though it were one's own.

P3Q18.q: Why does Aquinas locate the virtue of hope in the will rather than in the sensitive appetite (irascible)?
options: Because hope has no fixed subject at all
Because the principal object of the virtue of hope is a Divine, not a merely sensible, good, and only the higher, intellective appetite (the will) can be moved toward such a good without passion
Because the irascible appetite is incapable of any movement toward future goods
Because Aquinas holds hope is purely an act of the intellect, not the appetite
P3Q18.explanation: Since habits are known by their acts, and the act of hope as a theological virtue reaches for a Divine, not sensible, good, it must reside in the will (intellective appetite) rather than in the sensitive appetite, whose movements are always accompanied by passion.

P3Q18.q: Why, according to Aquinas, does theological hope not exist in the blessed in heaven?
options: Because the blessed have no appetite left at all

Because hope's species is taken from its principal object — eternal happiness as something still to be obtained — but the blessed already possess that happiness, so the very object that specifies hope is no longer future or unobtained for them
Because hope is replaced entirely by faith in heaven
Because charity eliminates the need for hope even before death
P3Q18.explanation: Since a virtue takes its species from its principal object, and hope's object is a future, not-yet-possessed good, the blessed who already possess eternal happiness no longer have an object for that species of hope.

P3Q18.q: How does Aquinas explain the certainty found in the hope of a person still on the earthly journey (a "wayfarer")?
options: Wayfarer's hope has no certainty whatsoever, unlike faith

Certainty exists essentially in a cognitive power and by participation in whatever is infallibly moved by it; hope shares by participation in the certainty of faith, the cognitive habit on which it depends, giving it real though derivative certainty
Hope is more certain than faith itself, since it concerns a more desirable object
Certainty in hope depends entirely on one's subjective feelings of confidence
P3Q18.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes essential certainty (in a cognitive power) from certainty by participation (in what is moved by that power); since hope is moved by faith's certainty toward its end, it shares that certainty by participation, even though hope itself is an act of appetite, not intellect.

P3Q19.q: How does Aquinas resolve the apparent contradiction that God is called the essence of goodness, yet Scripture commands us to fear Him?
options: He denies that Scripture actually commands fear of God

Fear's object can be either the evil itself feared, or the source from which evil may come; God cannot be feared in the first sense (as He is goodness itself) but can be feared in the second sense, insofar as some evil to us may relate to Him (e.g. as just judge)
God is feared only by those who reject the faith entirely
Fear of God is purely metaphorical and has no real object
P3Q19.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the evil feared from the source from which evil comes; since God is goodness itself He cannot be an object of fear in the first sense, but He can be feared in the second sense as the one from whom punishment for sin might come.

P3Q19.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that "worldly fear" — as opposed to filial or servile fear — is always evil?
options: Because it always leads to physical harm

Because it arises from worldly love, which treats the world as one's final end, and since that love is itself always disordered, the fear born from it (of losing worldly goods) is likewise always evil
Because fear itself, of any kind, is intrinsically sinful
Because worldly fear is identical to servile fear, which he judges to be evil too
P3Q19.explanation: Since fear is born of love (one fears losing what one loves), and worldly love — trusting in the world as one's end — is inherently disordered, the fear rooted in that same disordered love (worldly fear) is likewise always evil.

P3Q19.q: How does Aquinas explain that servile fear (fear of punishment) can coexist with charity?
options: It cannot; servile fear is always incompatible with charity

Fear of punishment proceeds from a legitimate self-love (not wanting to lose one's own good), and since loving one's own good is compatible with charity, so too is the resulting fear of losing that good through punishment
Servile fear is simply another name for filial fear
Charity actively produces servile fear as one of its effects
P3Q19.explanation: Aquinas reasons that fearing punishment stems from loving one's own good (self-love), which charity does not exclude; since it is fitting to love one's own good and fear its loss, servile fear so understood is compatible with charity.

P3Q20.q: Why does Aquinas classify despair as a sin, given that it is a movement of the appetite rather than a false belief in the intellect?
options: Despair is not actually a sin in Aquinas's account

Appetitive movements conform to true or false judgments of the intellect; since the true opinion is that God offers pardon and salvation to the repentant, despair, which conforms to the false opinion that God withholds pardon, is vicious just as hope conforming to the true opinion is virtuous
Despair is classified purely as an emotional disorder with no moral weight
Despair is sinful only when it leads to suicide
P3Q20.explanation: Following the Philosopher's parallel of intellect/appetite to truth/goodness, Aquinas holds that despair, conforming to the false belief that God refuses pardon to the repentant, is as vicious as hope (conforming to the true belief in God's mercy) is virtuous.

P3Q20.q: How can Aquinas say a person can fall into despair without also being an unbeliever?
options: This is impossible; despair always requires prior unbelief

Because unbelief concerns universal intellectual assent while despair concerns the particular appetitive estimate; one can retain the universal truth of faith (that the Church can forgive sins) while wrongly judging, in a corrupted particular estimate, that pardon is not available to oneself
Because despair and unbelief are simply two names for an identical sin
Because Aquinas holds despair only ever occurs in those outside the Church
P3Q20.explanation: Aquinas parallels this with the fornicator who retains the universal moral truth that fornication is wrong while choosing it in the particular; likewise, one can hold the universal truth of the Church's power to forgive while a corrupted particular estimate produces despair of one's own pardon.

P3Q20.q: Why does Aquinas connect despair especially to the vice of lust (among the causes he considers)?
options: Lust has no causal connection to despair in his account

Attachment to bodily, especially sexual, pleasures dulls one's taste for spiritual goods, making them seem less desirable or attainable, which undermines the hope that regards them as an arduous but obtainable good, thus producing despair
Despair is caused only by intellectual doubt, never by any moral vice
Lust and despair are simply identical in species for Aquinas
P3Q20.explanation: Aquinas explains that indulgence in bodily pleasures — especially sexual pleasure, which he says holds first place among these — dulls one's appetite for spiritual goods, making them seem unappealing or unattainable and thereby fostering despair.

P3Q21.q: According to Aquinas, presumption relying on one's own power is opposed to which virtue that holds the mean regarding great hopes?
options: Temperance
Magnanimity, since this presumption tends toward a good beyond one's real powers as though it were attainable by oneself
Justice
Prudence
P3Q21.explanation: Aquinas identifies this species of presumption — trusting immoderately in one's own power for a good beyond one's capacity — as opposed to magnanimity, the virtue that holds the mean in hoping for great things.

P3Q21.q: Why does Aquinas consider presumption a sin, paralleling his treatment of despair?
options: Presumption is not actually sinful, only imprudent
Like despair, presumption is an appetitive movement conformed to a false judgment — here, the false belief that God grants glory or pardon to those who persist in sin without repentance or effort
Presumption is sinful only when it leads to actual failure
Presumption is a purely intellectual error with no appetitive component
P3Q21.explanation: Just as despair conforms to the false belief that God withholds pardon, presumption conforms to the false belief that God grants forgiveness or glory to those who persevere in sin or cease good works, making it sinful in the same way.

P3Q21.q: According to Aquinas, from what vice does the presumption of attempting things beyond one's own power typically arise?
options: Sloth
Vainglory, since an excessive desire for glory and admiration, especially through novelties, drives one to attempt what exceeds one's ability
Envy
Avarice
P3Q21.explanation: Aquinas states that presumption of novelties is 'a daughter of vainglory,' since the desire for glory and admiration drives a person to attempt feats beyond his actual powers.

P3Q22.q: Why does Aquinas classify the precept of hope among the "preambles" to the Law rather than among precepts belonging to its substance?
options: Because hope is not actually commanded anywhere in Scripture

Because preambles to the Law are what make any law possible at all — faith disposes the mind to accept the Lawgiver's authority, and hope, through the promise of reward, induces observance of the precepts — whereas substantive precepts govern right conduct for those already subject and willing to obey
Because hope precepts were added only much later by the Church
Because Aquinas holds hope has no relevance to keeping the Law
P3Q22.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes preambles to the Law (which make submission to a lawgiver possible, like faith and hope) from precepts of the Law's substance (right conduct commanded of those already subject); hope's role in motivating obedience through the promise of reward places it among the preambles.

P3Q22.q: How does Aquinas parallel the precept of fear with the precept of hope in motivating obedience to the Law?
options: Fear plays no role comparable to hope
Just as hope of reward induces observance of precepts, servile fear of punishment likewise induces man to observe the precepts of the Law
Fear and hope are mutually exclusive motivations that cannot coexist in the same law
Only fear, never hope, is needed to secure obedience
P3Q22.explanation: Aquinas draws a direct parallel: as hope of reward induces observance of the law's precepts, so does servile fear of punishment serve the same motivating function, justifying a precept of fear alongside one of hope.

P3Q23.q: Why does Aquinas argue that charity must be a kind of friendship, rather than merely a form of love or desire?
options: Because friendship requires no reciprocity at all

Because according to the Philosopher, only love joined with benevolence — wishing good to another for the other's own sake — has the character of friendship, unlike love of concupiscence (as when we 'love' wine, wanting its good for ourselves), and charity is precisely this kind of mutual benevolent love toward God
Because Aquinas denies charity is a form of love in any sense
Friendship for Aquinas requires the two parties be socially equal, which excludes charity toward God
P3Q23.explanation: Aquinas follows Aristotle's distinction: love of concupiscence wants a good for oneself (as with wine), while love of friendship wishes good to another for their own sake with mutual benevolence; charity toward God fits the latter, since God communicates His happiness to us and there is a real mutual love.

P3Q23.q: According to Aquinas, why can no true virtue exist without charity?
options: Because all virtues are simply identical to charity

Because virtue is ordered to the good, and the ultimate, principal good of man is the enjoyment of God, to which man is ordered specifically by charity; anything not so ordered fails to be simply and truly virtuous
Because Aquinas holds pagans possessed no virtues whatsoever, contradicting his own later remarks
Because charity is merely one virtue among many with no special priority
P3Q23.explanation: Since true virtue must be directed to man's principal good — the enjoyment of God — and charity alone directs the soul to this ultimate end, Aquinas concludes that no virtue can be simply and truly virtue without being ordered to that end by charity.

P3Q23.q: In what sense does Aquinas call charity the "form" of the other virtues?
options: Charity is the physical shape or appearance of virtuous actions

In morals, the form of an act comes chiefly from the will's object, the end; since charity directs the acts of all other virtues to the last end (God), it gives those acts their moral form, making them fully virtuous ('informed') acts
Charity replaces the acts of the other virtues entirely
The term 'form' here refers only to liturgical formulas of charitable works
P3Q23.explanation: Because the form of a moral act follows from its ordering to an end, and charity orders every other virtuous act to the last end, charity is said to give form to the other virtues, making their acts 'informed' by charity rather than merely materially virtuous.

P3Q24.q: Why does Aquinas locate charity in the will rather than in the sensitive appetite?
options: Because charity is purely an intellectual habit with no appetitive dimension

Because charity's object is the Divine good grasped under its universal aspect by the intellect, not a good apprehended merely by sense, and only the will (intellective appetite) has such a good as its proper object
Because the will and the sensitive appetite are identical in Aquinas's psychology
Because charity, unlike hope, has no proper subject at all
P3Q24.explanation: Since the sensitive appetite's object is a sense-apprehended good while the will's object is good under its universal, intellectually-apprehended aspect, and charity's object is the Divine good known by intellect, charity resides in the will.

P3Q24.q: Why does Aquinas hold that charity cannot be acquired by natural human powers but must be infused by God?
options: Because charity is simply identical with natural self-love

Because charity is a friendship founded on the fellowship of everlasting happiness, which is a gratuitous, not a natural, gift, and an effect surpassing nature's proportion cannot be produced by natural powers, since a natural effect cannot transcend its cause
Because Aquinas believes all virtues, natural or supernatural, require infusion
Because the will alone can never produce any love, natural or supernatural
P3Q24.explanation: Since charity's foundation, the fellowship of everlasting (gratuitous, not natural) happiness, exceeds the proportion of human nature, and a natural cause cannot produce an effect beyond its own power, charity must come from the Holy Ghost's infusion rather than being acquired naturally.

P3Q24.q: What does Aquinas mean by saying charity can increase, and why is this essential to it as the virtue of a "wayfarer"?
options: Charity cannot increase once given; it is received in full or not at all

Since a wayfarer is one advancing on the way to God, and this approach to God is achieved through charity uniting the mind to Him, charity's ability to increase is essential — otherwise all further spiritual progress toward God would necessarily cease
Charity increases only through external ritual acts, never through interior acts of love
Aquinas holds increase in charity is impossible in this present life
P3Q24.explanation: Because we are called wayfarers as we advance toward God through the union charity effects, Aquinas argues charity's capacity to increase is essential to this journey — without it, further approach to God (spiritual advance) could not happen.

P3Q25.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that the love of charity extends beyond God to our neighbor as well, rather than stopping at God alone?
options: Because loving one's neighbor is a wholly separate virtue unrelated to charity

Because charity, as friendship with God, is directed to the fellowship of happiness God shares with rational creatures; since love of a friend naturally extends to those who share that friend's fellowship, the same charity that loves God also loves those who can share in His happiness
Because Scripture nowhere connects love of neighbor with love of God
Because loving one's neighbor is merely commanded separately with no essential link to loving God
P3Q25.explanation: Since acts are specified by their object under its formal aspect, and love of neighbor shares the very fellowship of happiness in God that charity toward God is based on, Aquinas concludes it is specifically the same charity extending to God and neighbor together, like seeing light and seeing color by that light.

P3Q25.q: Why does Aquinas deny that irrational creatures (like animals) can properly be loved with the love of charity, though we may care for them?
options: Because Aquinas believes animals have no value whatsoever

Because friendship (of which charity is a species) requires wishing genuine good to another as a possessor of good through free will, a shared life together, and above all the fellowship of everlasting happiness — none of which an irrational creature can have, so love of them is only love of concupiscence or metaphorical friendship
Because animals are incapable of any relationship with humans at all
Because charity is reserved exclusively for rational creatures already in a state of grace
P3Q25.explanation: Aquinas gives three reasons irrational creatures cannot be objects of the friendship of charity: they cannot properly possess good, cannot share a common rational life with us, and cannot attain the fellowship of everlasting happiness on which charity is founded.

P3Q25.q: What is Aquinas's resolution to whether we are bound out of charity to love our enemies?
options: We must love enemies precisely as enemies, approving the evil in them

We must not love the evil or enmity in them as such, but we can and should love them according to their nature and capacity for happiness, willing their good in general even while we may hate their sin or hostility
Charity forbids any love whatsoever toward one's enemies
Loving enemies is a counsel of perfection, not a strict requirement of charity for anyone
P3Q25.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes loving an enemy 'as such' (perverse, since it approves evil) from loving what is good in them (their nature, capacity for happiness); charity requires the latter, at least in the general disposition of the will, even toward those who oppose us.

P3Q26.q: According to Aquinas, why must there be an order among the things we love out of charity?
options: Because charity actually forbids any ranking among objects of love

Because wherever there is a principle, there must be order in reference to it, and since charity's love tends to God as the principle of happiness on which its fellowship is founded, the things loved out of charity must be ordered in reference to that first principle
Because civil law, not charity, determines the order of love
Order in love applies only to relationships among strangers, not family or God
P3Q26.explanation: Aquinas reasons from the general principle that wherever there is a source or principle, there is an order of before-and-after in reference to it; since charity's love is founded on God as the principle of the fellowship of happiness, an order among its objects necessarily follows.

P3Q26.q: Why does Aquinas argue that a person should love God more than himself, even above his own good of nature?
options: Because self-love is always sinful and must be entirely suppressed

Because natural love inclines every part to love the common good of the whole more than its own particular good — even irrational things exhibit this — so all the more should the friendship of charity, founded on the fellowship of grace, incline a person to love God, the common good, more than himself
Because Aquinas holds loving oneself is impossible under charity
Because Scripture explicitly ranks God above self only for clergy, not laity
P3Q26.explanation: Aquinas uses the analogy that every part naturally loves the good of the whole more than its own private good (seen even in inanimate and animal examples and in civic self-sacrifice); since charity is founded on an even higher fellowship (grace), it should incline us still more strongly to love God, the common good, above self.

P3Q26.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that a person should love his neighbor's spiritual welfare more than his own body?
options: Because the body has no value at all in Aquinas's anthropology

Because charity loves more what has fuller reason for being loved, and full participation in the fellowship of happiness (which is the reason for loving one's neighbor) is a greater reason for love than the mere overflow of that fellowship onto one's own body
Because Aquinas denies any obligation to care for one's own body
Because neighbors are always spiritually superior to oneself
P3Q26.explanation: Since one's neighbor fully shares in the fellowship of happiness that grounds charity's love while one's own body only shares by a kind of 'overflow,' Aquinas concludes the neighbor's spiritual good deserves greater love, out of charity, than one's own bodily good.

P3Q27.q: Why does Aquinas argue that "to love" is more proper to charity than "to be loved"?
options: Because being loved is impossible for anyone practicing charity

Because loving belongs to charity by its very essence as an inclination to its proper act, whereas being loved pertains to one only accidentally, insofar as another's act of charity tends toward one's good — as shown by the fact that friends are praised for loving, and a mother's love, the greatest kind, seeks to love rather than to be loved in return
Because being loved requires reciprocity which charity does not require at all
Because Aquinas holds loving and being loved are strictly identical acts
P3Q27.explanation: Since what belongs to a thing by its own essence is more proper to it than what belongs to it only through something else, and to love (not to be loved) is charity's own act by its essence, loving is more properly charity's than being loved — illustrated by how friends are praised for loving and a mother's love seeks to love rather than be loved back.

P3Q27.q: According to Aquinas, in what sense should God be loved "for Himself" rather than for some other reason?
options: God should never be loved for the sake of any benefit we might receive from Him

Considering the final, formal, and efficient senses of "for," God is loved for Himself because He is Himself the last end of all things, is goodness by His very substance rather than by acquiring some form, and is the source rather than recipient of goodness from anything else — though in a fourth, dispositive sense, He may also be loved on account of benefits that dispose us toward loving Him more
God is loved for Himself only in the beatific vision, never in this life
Aquinas denies it is ever proper to love God on account of any benefit
P3Q27.explanation: Analyzing the four senses of causal 'for,' Aquinas shows God is loved for Himself in the final, formal, and efficient senses (He is His own end, His own goodness, and its source), while benefits or hoped-for rewards may still dispose us toward loving Him more, in the fourth (material/dispositive) sense.

P3Q27.q: How does Aquinas resolve which is more meritorious: loving God, or loving one's neighbor for God's sake?
options: Loving one's neighbor is always more meritorious than loving God

Comparing the loves separately, love of God is more meritorious since it is rewarded for its own sake; but comparing love of God alone versus love of neighbor-for-God's-sake (which includes love of God), the latter, being the more perfect and complete love of God extending also to neighbor, is more meritorious than an inadequate, isolated love of God alone
The two loves are entirely incomparable and cannot be ranked
Neither love of God nor of neighbor is meritorious without accompanying good works
P3Q27.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes two comparisons: love of God alone is more meritorious than love of neighbor alone; but complete love of God that also extends to neighbor (per 1 John 4:21) is more perfect, and thus more meritorious, than an incomplete love of God that stops short of neighbor.

P3Q28.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that spiritual joy about God is caused by charity?
options: Because joy and charity are entirely unrelated psychological phenomena

Because joy arises from love through the presence or enduring good of the beloved, and since charity is love of God, Whose good is unchangeable, and Who dwells in those who love Him by His most excellent effect, spiritual joy about God necessarily follows from charity
Because joy is a purely bodily sensation with no connection to any virtue
Because Aquinas holds only despair, never joy, follows from love of God
P3Q28.explanation: Since joy is caused by love through the enduring presence of the good loved, and charity as love of God brings God's indwelling presence (per 1 John 4:16) to the one who loves, spiritual joy about God flows necessarily from charity.

P3Q28.q: According to Aquinas, why is the joy proper to charity — rejoicing in the Divine good considered in itself — entirely incompatible with any admixture of sorrow?
options: Because Aquinas denies believers can ever experience sorrow in this life
Because this joy's object, the Divine good, admits of no admixture of evil, and since joy conforms to its object, a joy about a good utterly free of evil cannot itself be mixed with sorrow
Because sorrow is impossible for any human being, according to Aquinas
Because this joy occurs only after death, when sorrow has ceased entirely
P3Q28.explanation: Since the Divine good rejoiced in for its own sake admits no admixture of evil, the joy of charity that rejoices in it directly is likewise incompatible with sorrow, as Aquinas notes citing Philippians 4:4, 'Rejoice in the Lord always.'

P3Q28.q: Why does Aquinas hold that joy is not a distinct virtue from charity, but merely an act or effect of it?
options: Because joy has no connection whatsoever to charity

Because when several ordered acts flow from one habit (as love, desire, and joy do from the same appetitive movement), the habit is named from the first of these acts — love — so the virtue is called charity, and joy is simply a subsequent act or fruit of that same virtue, not a separate one
Because Aquinas denies joy can ever be an effect of any virtue
Because joy, unlike love, is a purely passive experience unrelated to virtue
P3Q28.explanation: Since love is the first movement of the appetite from which desire and joy both flow, the virtue takes its name and definition from love (charity), while joy remains simply an act or fruit proceeding from that same virtuous habit, not a separate virtue.

P3Q29.q: How does Aquinas distinguish peace from mere concord?
options: They are entirely identical concepts with no distinction

Peace includes concord (agreement of appetites with one another) but adds something further to it — a tranquility resulting from the ordering of one's own internal desires as well — so all peace involves concord, but not all concord amounts to true peace
Concord is a broader term that always includes peace
Peace refers only to the absence of war between nations, unlike concord
P3Q29.explanation: Aquinas states that peace includes concord and adds something more to it; hence wherever there is peace there is concord, but concord alone (agreement without inner tranquility of order) does not amount to peace in its proper sense.

P3Q29.q: Why does Aquinas claim that all things, in desiring anything at all, thereby also desire peace?
options: Because desiring things and desiring peace are unrelated phenomena

Because to desire something is to desire to obtain it without hindrance, and this tranquil, unhindered attainment — removing whatever obstacles (one's own or another's contrary desires) — is precisely what peace, "the tranquility of order," consists in
Because Aquinas denies that desire and peace can coexist
Because only rational creatures, not all things, can desire peace
P3Q29.explanation: Since desiring a thing implies desiring to attain it with tranquility and without hindrance from contrary desires, and this undisturbed attainment is what Augustine's definition of peace as 'tranquility of order' describes, every desire implicitly includes a desire for peace.

P3Q29.q: Why does Aquinas identify peace as a proper effect of charity, involving a twofold union?
options: Peace has no real connection to charity in Aquinas's system

Charity effects peace in two ways: uniting one's own desires around a single object by loving God with one's whole heart, and uniting one's will with the neighbor's will by loving him as oneself, so that one wills to fulfill the neighbor's will as one's own
Peace results only from external legal agreements, not from any interior virtue
Charity produces discord, not peace, since it demands sacrifice
P3Q29.explanation: Aquinas explains peace's twofold union — the ordering of one's own appetites toward God as their single object, and the union of one's will with a neighbor's through loving him as oneself — as effects specifically produced by charity.

P3Q30.q: According to Aquinas, why is another person's evil or distress properly the motive that arouses mercy?
options: Because mercy is aroused by any change in another's circumstances, good or bad

Because mercy (misericordia) denotes a compassionate heart for another's unhappiness, and since happiness consists in having what one desires, unhappiness — suffering what one does not wish — is what specifically excites the heartfelt sympathy that is mercy
Because mercy arises only in response to physical, never spiritual or moral, evils
Because Aquinas denies that any particular kind of object arouses mercy
P3Q30.explanation: Since mercy is defined as heartfelt sympathy for another's distress, and unhappiness — suffering what is contrary to one's wishes — is opposed to the happiness of having what one desires, this unhappiness or evil is properly what excites mercy.

P3Q30.q: Under what condition does Aquinas conclude that mercy is a genuine virtue rather than a mere passion?
options: Mercy is always merely a passion and never rises to the level of virtue

When the grief for another's evil is not simply a movement of the sensitive appetite but a movement of the intellective appetite, ruled by reason in such a way that justice is safeguarded even as one gives to the needy or forgives the repentant
Mercy becomes a virtue only when it results in a specific canonically-mandated act of charity
Mercy is a virtue only in God, never in human beings
P3Q30.explanation: Aquinas, citing Augustine, holds that mercy is a virtue when this movement of the mind obeys reason — being exercised in a way that safeguards justice, whether in giving to the needy or forgiving the repentant — since virtue requires the soul's movements to be regulated by reason.

P3Q31.q: Why does Aquinas classify beneficence (doing good to others) as an act of charity rather than a distinct virtue?
options: Because beneficence and charity share no real connection

Because the will's love naturally seeks to carry its goodwill into effect, and since beneficence and charity share the same formal object (the common aspect of good), beneficence is simply charity's goodwill put into action, not a separate virtue
Because beneficence is purely a natural, not moral, phenomenon
Because Aquinas denies beneficence can ever proceed from love
P3Q31.explanation: Since love includes goodwill toward the one loved, and the will naturally carries its wishes into effect where possible, doing good to a friend follows from loving them; because beneficence and charity share the same formal object (the good), beneficence is an act of charity, not a distinct virtue.

P3Q31.q: According to Aquinas, should we be beneficent to everyone, and if so, how?
options: No, beneficence is owed only to family members
Yes — since the love of charity extends to all, beneficence should extend to all as well, but it must be modified according to due circumstances of time and place, as with any virtuous act
No, beneficence should be restricted exclusively to fellow believers
Yes, but only in the form of financial giving, never other kinds of help
P3Q31.explanation: Because beneficence flows from charity, which extends to everyone, Aquinas holds we should do good to all, though always tempered by the appropriate circumstances of time, place, and need, as all virtuous acts must be.

P3Q32.q: Why does Aquinas classify almsgiving specifically as an act of mercy (and thus of charity through mercy), rather than of some other virtue?
options: Because almsgiving is purely a legal obligation with no interior motive

Because the very motive for giving alms — relieving someone in need out of compassion and for God's sake — belongs properly to mercy, and since mercy is itself an effect of charity, almsgiving is an act of charity exercised through mercy
Because almsgiving is an act of justice, correcting an unequal distribution of goods
Because alms are given primarily to fulfill ecclesiastical law, not from any virtue
P3Q32.explanation: Aquinas notes that external acts belong to the virtue that supplies their motive; since alms are given out of compassion for the needy 'for God's sake,' this motive belongs to mercy, making almsgiving an act of charity through the mediating virtue of mercy.

P3Q32.q: According to Aquinas, why do spiritual almsdeeds generally hold a higher place than corporal almsdeeds, considered simply?
options: Because corporal almsdeeds are not really acts of mercy at all

For three reasons: the spiritual gift offered is more excellent, the soul that is succored is more excellent than the body, and the spiritual acts themselves are nobler than corporal, comparatively servile, acts
Because Aquinas holds only spiritual almsdeeds are commanded by precept
Because corporal almsdeeds always harm the giver more than they help the recipient
P3Q32.explanation: Aquinas gives three reasons for the general superiority of spiritual almsdeeds: the excellence of the gift itself, the excellence of the soul (the object helped) over the body, and the nobility of spiritual acts compared to more servile corporal ones.

P3Q32.q: Under what circumstance does Aquinas say it would be wrong to give away goods one needs for one's own or one's dependents' survival?
options: It is always praiseworthy to give away necessities, regardless of consequences

When doing so would endanger one's own life or that of those under one's charge in a situation of urgent necessity — though he allows an exception where risking oneself could preserve someone whose safety greatly serves the common good, such as an important support of Church or State
Aquinas denies any moral limit exists on almsgiving from necessities
One may never give from necessities under any circumstance whatsoever
P3Q32.explanation: Aquinas holds it is generally wrong to give away what is strictly necessary for one's own or dependents' survival, since this would recklessly endanger life, though he allows a praiseworthy exception when the common good is served by risking oneself to preserve someone of great public importance.

P3Q33.q: According to Aquinas, why is fraternal correction properly considered an act of charity?
options: Because it is primarily a matter of legal punishment

Because a person's sin can harm not only himself but others and the common good, and correction functions as a remedy applied for the good (amendment) of the sinner, which is precisely what charity, as love seeking the good of another, moves us to provide
Because correction is only ever practiced by Church prelates exercising jurisdiction
Because fraternal correction is primarily an act of justice, not love
P3Q33.explanation: Since sin harms both the sinner and potentially others, and correction serves as the remedy directed at the sinner's amendment (a good for him), Aquinas classifies fraternal correction as flowing from charity's concern for another's well-being.

P3Q33.q: Is fraternal correction, according to Aquinas, binding on every person at every possible time, like a negative precept?
options: Yes, exactly like a negative precept, it binds absolutely at all times and places

No — like other affirmative acts of virtue, it is a matter of precept only insofar as it is necessary for the brother's amendment, observing due circumstances of when, where, and how, not requiring correction at every place and time
No, fraternal correction is never actually obligatory, only optional
Yes, but only for those who hold formal positions of Church authority
P3Q33.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes negative precepts (binding always and everywhere) from positive/affirmative acts of virtue, which require due circumstances; fraternal correction, being a positive act, binds as necessary for a brother's correction but not indiscriminately at every time and place.

P3Q33.q: Can a subject licitly correct a prelate, according to Aquinas, and on what basis?
options: No, a subject may never in any way address a prelate's faults

Yes, though a subject cannot exercise the coercive correction proper to justice over a prelate, the fraternal correction that is an act of charity is within anyone's competency toward any person, prelate or not, bound to them by charity, when correction is warranted
Yes, but only if the subject holds equal or higher rank in civil society
No, because prelates are by definition incapable of sin requiring correction
P3Q33.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes correction as an act of justice (coercive, reserved to superiors) from fraternal correction as an act of charity (available to anyone toward anyone they are bound to love), meaning even a subject may fraternally correct a prelate when warranted.

P3Q34.q: Why does Aquinas argue it is impossible for someone who sees God in His Essence (the beatific vision) to hate Him?
options: Because such vision removes the will's freedom entirely
Because God's Essence is goodness itself, and it is natural for the good to be loved, not hated, so seeing God as He truly is (infinite goodness) precludes hatred of Him
Because hatred is impossible for any human being under any condition
Because Aquinas denies anyone can see God's Essence in this life or the next
P3Q34.explanation: Since hatred is an appetitive movement responding to what is apprehended as evil, and God seen in His Essence is goodness itself (which is naturally loved, not hated), Aquinas concludes direct vision of God's Essence excludes the possibility of hating Him.

P3Q34.q: According to Aquinas, why is hatred of one's neighbor sometimes not sinful, given that we are commanded to love our neighbor?
options: Hatred of neighbor is always sinful without exception in Aquinas's view

Because love is properly due to what a person holds from God (his nature and any grace), not to what he has of himself through sin, so hating the sin or injustice in a neighbor (as opposed to hating him as a person made by God) need not be a sin against charity
Because Aquinas holds no genuine obligation to love one's neighbor exists
Because sinning against a neighbor is never as serious as sinning against God, so it is permitted
P3Q34.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes what a person has from God (nature, grace — properly loved) from what he has from sin (properly hated); since hatred is evil only insofar as it opposes a due love, hating the sin rather than the God-given nature of a neighbor need not itself be sinful.

P3Q35.q: How does Aquinas define sloth, and what is distinctive about the kind of sorrow it involves?
options: Sloth is bodily fatigue from excessive physical labor

Sloth is an oppressive sorrow that weighs on the mind so heavily that a man wants to do nothing at all — specifically, per his later analysis, sorrow directed at spiritual good insofar as it is a Divine good, making it opposed to the joy that charity produces
Sloth is simply a synonym for laziness with no reference to sorrow
Sloth refers only to failure to attend religious services
P3Q35.explanation: Drawing on Damascene, Aquinas defines sloth as an oppressive sorrow that weighs down the mind, making a person disinclined to act; specifically, it is sorrow about spiritual, divine good, which makes it directly opposed to the joy that is charity's proper effect.

P3Q35.q: Under what condition does Aquinas hold that the movement of sloth becomes a mortal, rather than merely venial, sin?
options: Sloth is always only a venial sin, never mortal

When the movement remains only in the sensuality (as mere resistance of flesh against spirit) it is venial; but when it reaches the consent of reason, such that one deliberately detests and turns away from the Divine good, it becomes mortal, since the consummation of sin lies in reason's consent
Sloth becomes mortal the very first moment any feeling of laziness arises
Sloth is mortal only if it results in a specific external act of negligence
P3Q35.explanation: Following his general principle that mortal sin requires the consent of reason, Aquinas holds that sloth remaining a mere movement of sensuality (resisting spiritual effort) is venial, while sloth that reaches full rational consent in detesting the Divine good becomes mortal.

P3Q36.q: According to Aquinas, what distinguishes true envy from a similar-looking sorrow that is not sinful, such as grieving over an enemy's prosperity out of fear?
options: There is no real distinction; all sorrow over another's good is envy

True envy is sorrow specifically because another's good is perceived, as such, to diminish or overshadow one's own excellence or reputation, whereas grieving over another's prosperity from fear of resulting harm (an effect of fear, not envy) is a different, potentially blameless, kind of sorrow
Envy differs from other sorrow only by its intensity, not its object or cause
Aquinas holds all forms of sorrow over another's good are equally virtuous
P3Q36.explanation: Aquinas (following Aristotle) distinguishes sorrow over another's good that stems from fear of resulting harm to oneself (not envy, and not necessarily sinful) from properly envious sorrow, which grieves at another's good specifically because it is perceived as diminishing one's own excellence.

P3Q36.q: Why does Aquinas hold that envy is a mortal sin by reason of its genus?
options: Because envy always leads directly to physical violence

Because envy's object, like charity's, is our neighbor's good, but by contrary movement — charity rejoices in it while envy grieves over it — making envy directly contrary to charity, the source of the soul's spiritual life
Because envy is punished more severely than other sins under canon law
Because Aquinas denies envy is really a sin, only an imperfection
P3Q36.explanation: Since a sin's genus/species is taken from its object, and envy's object is a neighbor's good approached with a movement (grief) contrary to charity's (joy), Aquinas concludes envy is, in its genus, directly opposed to charity and therefore mortal.

P3Q37.q: How does Aquinas explain the sinfulness of discord in relation to charity's effect of concord?
options: Discord has no relationship to charity whatsoever

Concord results from charity uniting many hearts around one thing — chiefly the Divine good, and secondarily a neighbor's good — so discord, as opposition to this unity, is sinful precisely insofar as it opposes the concord charity produces
Discord is sinful only when it results in physical conflict
Discord is entirely a natural, amoral phenomenon of differing opinions
P3Q37.explanation: Since concord (a unity of wills around a shared good) is an effect of charity, Aquinas reasons that discord, as its opposite, is sinful precisely to the extent that it works against this charity-produced unity.

P3Q37.q: Why does Aquinas identify discord as a "daughter" of vainglory?
options: Discord and vainglory are entirely unrelated vices

Discord involves a disunion of wills where one clings inordinately to his own view over another's; when this preference for one's own way is excessive, it stems from pride and the desire for one's own glory, i.e., vainglory
Discord arises exclusively from doctrinal disagreements, unrelated to personal pride
Aquinas denies that discord has any traceable moral origin
P3Q37.explanation: Aquinas reasons that clinging obstinately to one's own opinion over another's, when done inordinately, reflects a preference for one's own view rooted in pride's desire for self-glory — hence discord is classed as arising from (a daughter of) vainglory.

P3Q38.q: How does Aquinas distinguish contention from discord?
options: They are entirely identical with no distinction
Discord denotes a contrariety of wills (an inward disunion), while contention signifies a contrariety of speech — the outward, verbal expression and defense of one's own opinion against another's
Contention refers only to written disputes, discord only to spoken ones
Discord is a virtue while contention is always a vice
P3Q38.explanation: Aquinas explains that just as discord is a contrariety of wills, contention is its counterpart in speech — the verbal 'tending against' another by defending contrary positions.

P3Q38.q: Why does Aquinas classify contention, like discord, as arising from vainglory?
options: Because contention has no connection to any other vice
