Because just as people hold discordantly to their own opinion inwardly out of a desire for self-glory, so they become contentious by defending that opinion in words for the same underlying motive of vainglory
Because contention is caused exclusively by intellectual error, not by any appetite
Because Aquinas holds contention arises from envy, not vainglory
P3Q38.explanation: Aquinas draws a direct parallel to his treatment of discord: since contentious speech defends the very opinion one clings to out of a desire for one's own glory, contention is reckoned a daughter of vainglory for the same reason as discord.

P3Q39.q: Why does Aquinas classify schism as a special, distinct sin rather than a mere form of some other vice?
options: Because schism is simply identical to heresy in every respect

Because schism is directly and essentially opposed to the unity that charity produces — both binding individuals together and binding the whole Church in unity of spirit — and the schismatic specifically intends to sever himself from that unity, which makes it a sin with its own proper object
Because schism concerns only administrative, not spiritual, matters
Because schism is merely an accidental side effect of other sins, not intended in itself
P3Q39.explanation: Since the moral species of an act is determined by what is intended, and the schismatic specifically intends to break the unity of spirit that charity produces in the Church, Aquinas concludes schism is a special sin, properly and essentially opposed to that ecclesial unity.

P3Q39.q: According to Aquinas, does a bishop or priest who falls into schism lose the sacramental power he received through consecration?
options: Yes, sacramental power is entirely erased the moment someone becomes schismatic

No — sacramental power, once conferred by consecration, remains in the person as long as he lives (shown by the fact that he is not re-consecrated upon returning to the Church), though he loses the right to lawfully use that power while in schism
Sacramental power was never real for schismatics to begin with
Sacramental power depends entirely on continued communion and vanishes and returns as membership changes
P3Q39.explanation: Aquinas argues that sacramental power, conferred by an unrepeatable consecration, remains in the person as an indelible reality even in schism or heresy (proven by there being no re-consecration on return), while the lawful use of that power is nonetheless forfeited during the schism.

P3Q40.q: What three conditions does Aquinas require for a war to be just?
options: A declaration of intent, a formal treaty, and the consent of the enemy
The authority of the sovereign under whose command it is waged, a just cause (some fault on the part of those attacked), and a rightful intention (the advancement of good or the avoidance of evil)
Overwhelming military superiority, a papal blessing, and popular approval by referendum
A written constitution, standing armies only, and prior notification of neutral nations
P3Q40.explanation: Aquinas lists three requirements for a just war: it must be waged on the authority of a sovereign responsible for the common good (not a private individual), for a just cause, and with a right intention aimed at promoting good or avoiding evil, not mere aggrandizement or cruelty.

P3Q40.q: Why does Aquinas say a private individual has no authority to declare war?
options: Because private individuals lack the physical strength required for combat

Because a private person can seek redress for his rights from the tribunal of a superior, and it is the business of those charged with the care of the common weal — not private persons — to have recourse to the sword in defending it against internal or external threats
Because Aquinas holds that only the Pope may authorize any war whatsoever
Because private citizens are, by natural law, incapable of injustice, so no cause for war could arise for them
P3Q40.explanation: Aquinas reasons that a private individual, unlike a sovereign charged with the common good, can seek justice through a superior's court rather than the sword, and it is specifically those entrusted with public authority who may licitly resort to war in defense of the common weal.

P3Q40.q: According to Aquinas, is it ever lawful to use stratagems or ambushes against an enemy in war?
options: No, all forms of deception in warfare are absolutely forbidden without exception

Yes, provided the deception does not involve breaking one's word or promises — since no one may deceive by lying or violating covenants (which must be kept even toward enemies), but concealing one's plans or intentions (ambush) is lawful
No, Aquinas holds warfare must always be announced and telegraphed in advance
Yes, any form of deception whatsoever, including broken oaths, is permitted in a just war
P3Q40.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes deceiving an enemy through false statements or broken promises (always unlawful, since certain rights and covenants must be honored even with enemies) from concealing one's own plans through ambush, which he holds is a legitimate tactic in a just war.

P3Q41.q: How does Aquinas define strife, and why does he consider it always sinful in the aggressor?
options: Strife is merely a verbal disagreement, never physical

Strife is a contradiction extending to deeds, a kind of private war waged not by public authority but by an inordinate will, so it is always sinful in one who attacks another unjustly, since inflicting harm on another by one's own hands without just cause is not without mortal sin
Strife refers only to disputes among clergy over doctrine
Strife is never actually sinful, only regrettable
P3Q41.explanation: Aquinas defines strife as a kind of private war carried out by deeds rather than public authority, and holds that whoever unjustly attacks another in this way commits mortal sin, since inflicting unjust harm by one's own hands is gravely wrong.

P3Q41.q: According to Aquinas, can a person who defends himself against an unjust attacker be entirely free from sin?
options: No, self-defense is always at least a venial sin

Yes — if his sole intention is to resist the injury done to him and he defends himself with due moderation, there is no sin and this is not properly called strife at all; only if defense is driven by vengeance or exceeds moderation does it become sinful
No, any physical resistance to an attacker is automatically mortally sinful
Yes, but only if the attacker is killed in the process
P3Q41.explanation: Aquinas holds that moderate self-defense aimed solely at warding off injury involves no sin and is not properly strife; sin enters only when the defense is motivated by vengeance/hatred or exceeds due moderation, becoming venial or even mortal depending on degree.

P3Q42.q: How does Aquinas distinguish sedition from both war and strife?
options: Sedition is identical to strife, just involving more people

Sedition can denote either actual aggression or mere preparation for it (unlike war and strife, which denote actual aggression), and unlike war (between separate peoples) or strife (between individuals), sedition properly occurs between mutually dissenting parts of one and the same people
Sedition refers exclusively to religious uprisings, unlike war or strife
There is no meaningful distinction; Aquinas uses the terms interchangeably
P3Q42.explanation: Aquinas notes sedition can include mere preparation for conflict (not just actual aggression like war and strife) and, unlike war (between peoples) or strife (between individuals), properly occurs within a single people split into opposing factions.

P3Q42.q: Why does Aquinas classify sedition as a mortal sin by reason of its genus?
options: Because it inevitably leads to bloodshed

Because sedition is opposed to the unity of law and common good that constitutes a genuine 'people,' and so it is opposed to justice and the common good, with its gravity increasing as the common good it assails exceeds the private good assailed by mere strife
Because it is always directed against legitimate civil authority specifically
Because sedition is a purely private vice with no bearing on the common good
P3Q42.explanation: Drawing on Augustine's definition of a 'people' as a community united by law and common good, Aquinas argues that sedition attacks precisely this unity, making it opposed to justice and the common good and therefore graver than strife, which harms only private goods.

options: Any public embarrassment caused by immoral behavior
Something less rightly said or done that occasions another's spiritual downfall — like an obstacle in someone's path that causes them to stumble and fall
A synonym for any sin whatsoever, public or private
A purely legal term referring to defamation
P3Q43.explanation: Drawing on the Greek skandalon (an obstacle causing one to stumble), Aquinas defines scandal as something less rightly said or done which becomes an occasion for another's spiritual downfall.

P3Q43.q: According to Aquinas, why can "passive scandal" (being scandalized) never occur in someone who is spiritually perfect and adheres wholly to God?
options: Because perfect people are incapable of witnessing others' bad behavior

Because passive scandal implies the mind is unsettled in its adherence to good, but one who adheres firmly and immovably to God (Whose goodness is unchangeable) cannot be shaken from righteousness by others' apparent misconduct, however scandalous it may seem to weaker souls
Because Aquinas holds that scandal is always active, never passive, in perfect people
Because perfect people are legally exempt from being affected by others' sins
P3Q43.explanation: Since being scandalized requires one's adherence to good to be unsettled, and the perfect adhere immovably to God's unchangeable goodness (rather than merely to fallible human examples), they cannot be genuinely destabilized in their righteousness by others' apparent faults.

P3Q43.q: According to Aquinas, should one ever forego something necessary for one's own salvation merely to avoid scandalizing someone else?
options: Yes, avoiding scandal always takes precedence over one's personal salvation

No — because the order of charity requires a man to love his own spiritual welfare more than another's, so one should never commit even venial or mortal sin (by omitting something necessary for salvation) merely to prevent another's sin arising from scandal
Yes, but only if the person scandalized is a Church superior
No, spiritual goods are never a relevant consideration in questions of scandal
P3Q43.explanation: Aquinas reasons from the order of charity, which places a proper love of one's own spiritual welfare above concern for another's, concluding that things necessary for one's own salvation should never be foregone merely to avoid giving passive scandal to another.

P3Q44.q: According to Aquinas, why is the precept of charity the greatest of all the precepts?
options: Because it is the easiest precept to fulfill

Because charity — union with God, the end of the spiritual life — is due for its own sake, while other things (regulating passions, ensuring a good conscience, right faith) are due for the sake of reaching that union, and what is due for its own sake always takes precedence over what is due for the sake of something else
Because it was given directly by Christ rather than through Moses
Because all other precepts are optional, unlike the precept of charity
P3Q44.explanation: Aquinas argues that since union with God through charity is the very end of the spiritual life, sought for its own sake, while other virtues serve as means toward that end, and what is due for its own sake takes priority, charity's precept is the greatest of all.

P3Q44.q: Why does Aquinas hold it was fitting to give two distinct precepts of charity — love of God and love of neighbor — rather than one alone?
options: Because love of God and love of neighbor are entirely unrelated obligations

Because although love of neighbor is virtually contained within the precept to love God as its principle, not everyone easily grasps everything implicit in a general precept, so for the sake of those less able to draw out such implications, both precepts needed to be stated explicitly
Because Aquinas denies that love of neighbor is connected to love of God at all
Because Church law required two separate precepts for legal reasons
P3Q44.explanation: Since practical precepts relate to their end as conclusions relate to principles, and not everyone can readily see all that is virtually contained in a principle, Aquinas explains both love of God and love of neighbor needed to be commanded explicitly for those less intellectually capable of deriving one from the other.

P3Q44.q: According to Aquinas, can the precept to love God "with thy whole heart" be perfectly fulfilled in this present life?
options: Yes, perfect fulfillment is fully attainable by anyone striving with sufficient discipline in this life

No — perfect fulfillment (complete union in which God is 'all in all') is reserved for heaven, though the precept can still be fulfilled imperfectly on the earthly journey, in the sense that one's love is not turned away from its due order toward that end, with some persons approaching this perfection more than others
Yes, and Aquinas holds this precept was already perfectly fulfilled by the patriarchs of the Old Testament
No, the precept can never be fulfilled at all, even imperfectly, before death
P3Q44.explanation: Using the analogy of a general's command being perfectly obeyed by soldiers who achieve victory but imperfectly (though genuinely) obeyed by those who fight loyally without yet winning, Aquinas holds the precept of loving God wholly is perfectly fulfilled only in heaven, though it is genuinely, if imperfectly, fulfilled by wayfarers who do not depart from its order.

P3Q45.q: According to Aquinas, what distinguishes the gift of wisdom, which judges according to God as the highest cause "simply," from being wise merely "in a genus" (like medicine or architecture)?
options: There is no real distinction; all wisdom is of the same kind

One who knows the highest cause within some particular field can judge and order things within that field, but one who knows the cause that is simply the highest — God — is able to judge and order all things whatsoever according to Divine rules, making him wise simply, not merely in a restricted domain
Wisdom in a genus is always superior to wisdom "simply"
The gift of wisdom concerns only intellectual disciplines like philosophy, not everyday judgment
P3Q45.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes wisdom as expertise judging within a restricted field (like medicine) from wisdom 'simply,' which judges and orders all things according to knowledge of God, the absolutely highest cause — this latter is the gift of wisdom.

P3Q45.q: How does Aquinas explain that the gift of wisdom involves a kind of "connaturality" with divine things, distinct from mere reasoned inquiry?
options: Connaturality has nothing to do with the gift of wisdom

Just as a chaste person judges rightly about chastity by a kind of connaturality (from having the virtue itself) rather than solely by reasoned inquiry, the gift of wisdom judges rightly about Divine things through a union with them that is the effect of charity, not merely through systematic study
Connaturality refers only to an inherited biological trait, unrelated to virtue
Wisdom of this kind arises purely from formal philosophical training
P3Q45.explanation: Aquinas uses the analogy of a virtuous person's connatural, felt judgment about matters within that virtue (e.g., a chaste person's judgment about chastity) to explain how the gift of wisdom judges rightly about Divine things through the loving union with God that charity produces, rather than solely through discursive reasoning.

P3Q46.q: How does Aquinas explain the difference between folly as mere natural incapacity and folly as a sin?
options: Folly is always a sin, regardless of its cause

Folly arising from a natural indisposition, as in the case of idiots, is no sin; but folly caused by a person plunging his sense into earthly things until it becomes incapable of perceiving Divine things (like a corrupted sense of taste finding no savor in sweetness) is sinful
Folly is never sinful under any circumstance whatsoever
Folly refers exclusively to intellectual errors in mathematics or logic
P3Q46.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes folly from natural causes (like idiocy, not sinful) from folly resulting from a person culpably immersing his sense-judgment in earthly things until it can no longer perceive spiritual realities, which he does consider sinful.

P3Q46.q: Why does Aquinas identify lust as the chief source of the sinful kind of folly?
options: Lust has no particular connection to folly among the vices

Because man's sense is plunged into earthly things chiefly through lust, which concerns the greatest bodily pleasures, and these absorb the mind more than any other pleasures, thereby dulling the spiritual sense's capacity to judge divine things
Because folly and lust are simply two names for the same single vice
Because lust is the only vice Aquinas considers a sin at all
P3Q46.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since lust concerns the most absorbing bodily pleasures, it is chiefly responsible for immersing a person's sense-judgment in earthly things, thereby dulling the spiritual perception needed to judge divine matters — hence folly's chief source is lust.

P3Q47.q: Why does Aquinas locate prudence in the reason (cognitive faculty) rather than in the appetite?
options: Because prudence is purely a matter of feeling, unrelated to knowledge

Because prudence, per Isidore, involves 'seeing as it were from afar' and foreseeing uncertain future outcomes by comparing present or past knowledge, and this kind of foresight through comparison belongs properly to reason, a cognitive power, not to appetite
Because Aquinas denies prudence has any relationship to action at all
Because prudence and appetite are, for Aquinas, simply identical faculties
P3Q47.explanation: Following Isidore's description of the prudent man as one who foresees uncertain future events through comparison of present and past knowledge, Aquinas concludes this foreseeing function belongs to the cognitive power of reason, not to the appetitive faculty.

P3Q47.q: According to Aquinas, why must a prudent person have knowledge of particular, singular facts, not merely universal moral principles?
options: Because universal principles are entirely irrelevant to prudence

Because prudence's proper work includes not just rational consideration but the application of that consideration to concrete action, and since actions always concern singular, particular matters, one cannot rightly apply universal principles without also knowing the singular circumstances to which they must be applied
Because Aquinas denies that any universal moral principles exist
Because singular facts alone, without any universal principles, are sufficient for prudent action
P3Q47.explanation: Since prudence's aim is application of reason to concrete action, and actions always occur amid particular circumstances, Aquinas argues the prudent person must know both universal principles and the relevant singular facts in order to apply the former rightly to real situations.

P3Q47.q: Why does Aquinas identify "command" as the chief act of prudence, rather than "counsel" or "judgment"?
options: Because command alone, without counsel or judgment, constitutes the entirety of prudence

Because among the three acts involved in practical reasoning — taking counsel (inquiry), judging what has been discovered, and commanding (applying what was counseled and judged to actual performance) — command comes closest to the actual end of practical reason, which is action itself, making it prudence's chief and defining act
Because command is an act of the speculative, not the practical, reason
Because Aquinas denies that counsel or judgment are acts of prudence at all
P3Q47.explanation: Aquinas identifies three acts of practical reason — counsel, judgment, and command — and argues command is chief because it is the act that actually applies counseled and judged matters to action, which is the very purpose (end) of practical reason and thus of prudence.

P3Q48.q: According to Aquinas, how are the eight "integral parts" of prudence divided in relation to knowledge?
options: All eight parts concern only the acquisition of knowledge, with none pertaining to action

Five parts pertain to prudence as a cognitive virtue (memory, reasoning, understanding, docility, shrewdness), while three others pertain to its role commanding and applying knowledge to action (foresight, circumspection, and caution)
All eight parts are entirely unrelated to one another with no organizing principle
There are only three integral parts, not eight, in Aquinas's actual enumeration
P3Q48.explanation: Aquinas organizes the eight integral parts of prudence around three aspects of knowledge and its use: memory (of the past) and understanding (of the present), the acquiring of knowledge (docility and shrewdness), and its use in reasoning, plus three parts (foresight, circumspection, caution) belonging to prudence's commanding, action-applying role.

P3Q49.q: Why does Aquinas consider memory a necessary part of prudence?
options: Memory has no real bearing on prudent action

Prudence deals with contingent matters known through what holds true 'in the majority of cases,' which requires experience to discover, and since experience is the product of accumulated memories, prudence necessarily requires the memory of many things
Memory is required only for speculative knowledge, never for practical action
Aquinas holds that memory actually impedes prudent judgment
P3Q49.explanation: Since prudence concerns contingent action-matters known through what generally holds true, and such knowledge comes from experience, which is itself built up from many remembered instances, Aquinas concludes memory is essential to prudence.

P3Q49.q: Why does Aquinas count "docility" (a readiness to be taught) among the parts of prudence?
options: Because docility is unrelated to acquiring the particular knowledge prudence requires

Because the particular matters of action prudence must consider are of infinite variety and cannot be sufficiently grasped by any one person alone or quickly, so a person greatly needs to be taught by others, especially the experienced and elderly, making a disposition to be readily taught (docility) essential to prudence
Because docility refers to intellectual passivity, which Aquinas considers a vice rather than a virtue
Because docility is required only for those in positions of civil authority
P3Q49.explanation: Since the countless particular matters relevant to prudent action cannot be mastered by one person's experience alone or quickly, Aquinas holds that being well-disposed to learn from others, especially the experienced, is a necessary part (docility) of prudence.

P3Q50.q: Why does Aquinas hold that "regnative" prudence — the prudence of a king governing a kingdom — represents prudence in its most perfect and special sense?
options: Because a king's prudence requires no cooperation with subjects at all

Because government is more perfect the more universal it is, extending to more matters and attaining a higher end, and a king's governance of an entire city or kingdom (rather than merely himself) exemplifies this most perfect and universal kind of governance, to which the fullest form of prudence corresponds
Because regnative prudence is entirely unrelated to ordinary prudence directed at one's own good
Because Aquinas denies any distinctions among types of prudence
P3Q50.explanation: Since a more universal and higher-reaching governance constitutes a more perfect kind of rule, and a king governs an entire city or kingdom rather than merely himself, Aquinas concludes that regnative prudence — directed to this most universal common good — represents prudence's most perfect and special form.

P3Q50.q: Why does Aquinas argue that subjects, not just rulers, need their own kind of prudence (which he calls "political" prudence)?
options: Because subjects have no real need for prudence, since they are merely passive recipients of commands

Because unlike irrational or inanimate beings, which are simply moved by external movers with no self-direction, human subjects move themselves by free will even while obeying commands, so they require some rectitude of self-government in order to rightly direct themselves in obeying their superiors
Because political prudence applies only to rulers, contrary to what the article concludes
Because prudence in subjects is identical in every respect to regnative prudence in kings
P3Q50.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes human subjects, who move themselves by free will even under command, from irrational beings simply moved by external movers; because subjects must rightly direct their own free compliance, they need a specific kind of prudence (political prudence) for governing themselves well in obedience.
